title: Move to rejoin EU among options for UK, says Andy Burnham
description: Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Burnham said he did not want to leave the question of the EU relationship "hanging" and he wanted to be cle
body: Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Burnham said he did not want to leave the question of the EU relationship "hanging" and he wanted to be clear on "where we want Britain to go in the next decade".Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, he replied that he wanted to "look at the options".He added he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now"."We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," he told the programme."We could look at what [former Chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.""So there are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each," he added.Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said his party has put forward "concrete plans to boost our economy, strengthen our defences and cut people's taxes by joining the single market and a customs union".He added: "Talk is cheap. Burnham must stop with all the 'maybes' and get negotiating that better deal for Britain today."Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door".Tice said: "He says Brexit has done more harm than good but what's done real harm is a Labour government that can't deliver growth, can't control migration and now wants to outsource the job to Brussels."He added Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham blamed Brexit for a loss of control over both immigration and the economy, telling delegates he did not believe the current relationship was "good enough".He told activists he wanted to use the rescheduled summit later this year to lay out "different options" for the UK's long-term relationship with Europe.He promised to "find consensus" on an option to clarify the UK's position, although did not offer further detail of how this would be measured.In response to Burnham's conference speech, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "Labour cannot pin the blame for their disastrous economic decisions on a vote that happened over a decade ago."Besides, they are already dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset."

schema.headline: Move to rejoin EU among options for UK, says Andy Burnham

title: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
description: Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.She told the BBC it was
body: Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men"."I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.In the latest development -  first reported by the Times newspaper - it is claimed the suspect called police almost an hour before a local farmer also raised the alarm.A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation. "The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday."I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.

schema.headline: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself

title: Trent Alexander-Arnold: It is time for Thomas Tuchel to trust Real Madrid right-back
description: England head coach Thomas Tuchel's apparent lack of trust in Trent Alexander-Arnold has been one of the defining features - and a constant narrative -
body: England head coach Thomas Tuchel's apparent lack of trust in Trent Alexander-Arnold has been one of the defining features - and a constant narrative - of his time in charge.The 27-year-old right-back has won a Premier League title at Liverpool then moved to Real Madrid since he last started for England, selected as a left-back by interim manager Lee Carsley when scoring in a 3-1 Nations League win in Finland in October 2024.He was ignored for England's World Cup squad last summer, despite right-back being a cursed role for Tuchel, making it appear that whatever questions the German had about that position, Alexander-Arnold was never going to be the answer.So Tuchel's decision to recall Alexander-Arnold for this four-game Nations League camp came as a surprise, so emphatically had he been marginalised by England.It was against this backdrop that Alexander-Arnold became the ninth right-back used by Tuchel in 24 games when he finally got his start against Czech Republic in Prague as England tried to recover from the 3-2 loss to World Cup holders Spain at Wembley.And, with perhaps something to prove according to Tuchel, Alexander-Arnold did exactly that in one world-class moment that might convince his coach to train his sights on what he can do rather than what he cannot.It is time, in other words, for Tuchel to offer Alexander-Arnold some trust.England, despite being in control, were toiling against the 10-man Czechs, who had seen danger man Pavel Sulc sent off after only 25 minutes for a reckless challenge on Elliot Anderson.It was then, two minutes after the break, that Alexander-Arnold delivered a moment beyond those Tuchel has chosen ahead of him at right-back to pierce that stubborn resistance.The player now officially known as "Trent", according to the name on the back of his shirt, had already made a 70-yard run into an attacking position in an attempt to increase England's attacking options.When the move broke down, he regained possession before unfurling a magnificent right-foot delivery that floated in a teasing arc beyond three Czech defenders for Anthony Gordon to score with a stooping header that he made look far easier than it actually was.Of course, Tuchel may still harbour those reservations about Alexander-Arnold's defending, and they were not put to the test here, but these few seconds showed exactly what he is about and what he can rightly argue is his unique selling point.The defensive questions must wait for another day. The answers, whenever they come, would appear to shape Tuchel's thinking and Alexander-Arnold's England career, but he deserves the opportunity to provide them.A delighted Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He (Alexander-Arnold) did very well. He had an excellent assist. Overall, like everyone, he was professional, top attitude and one decisive action."He added: "We never doubted that he can produce these kinds of assists. The deeper position in the second half suited him more than the higher position in the first half."Overall, I think we had a good and professional performance. Of course, the red card, especially an early red card, is such a heavy influence in the game. It makes the task sometimes a little bit more complicated psychologically."Gordon, the grateful beneficiary of Alexander-Arnold's class, said: "I make that run time and time again and only a certain number of players have that ability, technique and bravery to be willing to make the mistake trying that pass. That's why he's so good and I've been dying to play with him for that reason."He's had his own journey with England. He would've liked to have played more than he has but he's been a great character during this camp. I've really enjoyed being around him."Alexander-Arnold is a risk taker, both in the defensive and attacking context, but only Elliot Anderson (41) made more passes in the final third than he did (32), while only Anthony Gordon, with four, created more chances than the defender's three.Tuchel, it should be stated, is not alone in having doubts about Alexander-Arnold.Who can forget – although many would love to – Sir Gareth Southgate's ill-fated attempt to utilise Alexander-Arnold as a midfielder at Euro 2024? It was ditched after 54 minutes of England's second game against Denmark never to be seen again.More will be revealed if Tuchel persists with Alexander-Arnold against Croatia behind closed doors in Rijeka on Saturday – but this must be close to make or break time for this lavishly-talented player who is 28 on 7 October.If he cannot convince Tuchel in this camp, and surely that one moment of game-changing skill must be fixed in the head coach's mind, then you wonder if he ever will.Alexander-Arnold said: "It was amazing. It's always an honour to represent my country. It's been a long time, but I've always believed I can play for England. That belief has always been there and it was about proving it at club level. The manager gave me a chance, now hopefully he is happy with how I played."How happy? Time, and Tuchel, will tell.Alexander-Arnold, however, could not have done any more as England, who sealed the three points with captain Harry Kane's 87th goal in 123 international appearances, got their Nations League campaign going in Prague.

schema.headline: Trent Alexander-Arnold: It is time for Thomas Tuchel to trust Real Madrid right-back

title: Motorists in Wales face fines of up to £150 for idling
description: Drivers in Wales who leave their vehicle engine running while parked will face fines of up to £150 from Wednesday. The change is part of a new measure
body: Drivers in Wales who leave their vehicle engine running while parked will face fines of up to £150 from Wednesday. The change is part of a new measure by the Welsh government to try to reduce harmful pollution and to protect children's health.The previous punishment for idling, as it is known, was £20, but that has now been raised to anywhere from £75 to £150, depending on circumstances.The Welsh government said it hoped the increase would "change the habits of people who are polluting communities".Llyr Gruffydd, cabinet minister for rural resilience and sustainability, said the £20 fixed fine for idling was "insufficient", and not being used "in the way everyone might envision it".Increasing the fee that is available for local authorities to penalise drivers will be a "stronger deterrent", he added. "We really do feel we need to step up here, clamp down on this as a problem and make sure we protect people's health and generally it will make communities a better place to live in."Gruffydd said he hoped the higher range of fines would "change the habits of people who are polluting communities and are putting children and vulnerable people's health at risk". Under rule 123 of the Highway Code, drivers must not leave a parked vehicle unattended with the engine running or leave a vehicle engine running unnecessarily while that vehicle is stationary on a public road. Areas outside schools have been identified as high risk sites where emissions pose particular concerns.Hospitals, GP surgeries, care homes and other healthcare facilities are also identified as high risk locations. Professor Isabel Oliver, chief medical officer for Wales, said air pollution was a serious public health issue that contributed to a range of conditions including heart and lung disease. "Children, older people and those with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable to its effects," she said."Idling may seem like a small, everyday habit, but it adds up. "Every time an engine is switched off rather than left running, we reduce the amount of harmful pollution in the air we all breathe, particularly around schools, hospitals and other places where vulnerable people spend time."This new measure comes into force following a vote at the Senedd in March. MSs passed the new rules, with 37 politicians voting for and 12 against. There were no abstentions.

schema.headline: Motorists in Wales face fines of up to £150 for idling

title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
description: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how
body: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning."Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

schema.headline: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons

title: Social anxiety: The hidden habits that make it worse - and how you can break them
description: Mary, who is now 25, describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face a
body: Mary, who is now 25, describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face and her hands would begin to tingle. "I'd almost feel myself separating from my body. I forgot how to form words," she says."After social situations I was often left with the sense that I'd done something awful. I had an all-consuming feel of shame. I kept thinking there was something fundamentally flawed in me."Neil Greening, chair of the Social Anxiety Alliance UK, says this is a typical characteristic of people with social anxiety."People think they have a personality flaw. They internalise it rather than seeing it as a recognisable condition that they can get help for."The key thing to remember: It's fairly normal to feel a little shy or anxious when meeting new people, being in new situations or going for a job interview. Social anxiety is when it actually stops people doing things, Greening says.For those with a clinical diagnosis it can have a debilitating impact like it did for Mary."It can be hard to admit to any form of social anxiety in a world where extrovertism and social confidence is generally admired. Many people try to hide their social anxiety or use safety behaviours."Signs someone may be socially anxious:Keeping quietGiving short answersPlaying with a phone to avoid interactingAlways staying close to someone or staying on the edges of a groupSticking to safe subjects of conversation like workGreening says there is some evidence social anxiety is getting worse and that increased use of smartphones and remote working is contributing by "leading to less social interactions and increased levels of anxiety".Mary, who has moved on to do a postgraduate course, is now managing her social anxiety better. After her undergraduate degree she got support from the NHS in the form of a talking therapy called CBT.It is considered the gold standard treatment for social anxiety and encourages people to re-frame their thoughts and change their behaviours.Prof David Clark, a psychologist at the University of Oxford, says he would like to see more people come forward for therapy but says people can also take steps to help themselves.The first step, he says, is to stop obsessive self-focus. "People with social anxiety often monitor themselves constantly during social situations. Am I blushing? Do I sound stupid? Do I look nervous?"Focus outwardly on the conversation, other person or your surroundings."He says you also need to test your fears with behavioural experiments by asking a question in a meeting or saying something in a group and noticing what happens."People with social anxiety often assume negative outcomes – that they will embarrass themselves or think others will find them boring. Testing that can help people break that. It's frightening, but it can really help."He also says they need to drop safety behaviours, such as rehearing every sentence, avoiding eye contact or sticking close to one particular person.And finally, Clark adds, try to avoid post-event rumination. "It's so easy to distort what actually happened."This is something Mary can empathise with. "I used to play things over constantly in my mind. What I've learnt is that dealing with social anxiety is a gradual process. The therapy really helped me, but so did something a friend said to me a couple of years ago."When I said I didn't want to join her in meeting some of her friends, citing my poor social skills, she said she'd never thought that about me and that I shouldn't undersell myself. I was overcome with emotion."I'm now pushing myself to engage more. It helps that in my postgrad course we're in smaller groups, but I've also joined an astronomy group. It's still difficult and it doesn't always go how I want it to, but I'm learning to manage it."

schema.headline: Social anxiety: The hidden habits that make it worse - and how you can break them

title: Antisemitism on the rise at universities, charity warns
description: Cases of antisemitism affecting university students and staff in the UK increased in the last academic year, according to a charity that monitors anti
body: Cases of antisemitism affecting university students and staff in the UK increased in the last academic year, according to a charity that monitors antisemitic incidents.The Community Security Trust (CST) said it had recorded 95 "university-related" incidents in the 2025-26 academic year - up from 83 the year before.It said the number had fallen from its peak in the year after Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza began, but remains "substantially higher" than before that point.Universities UK (UUK) represents more than 140 institutions and said its members needed to "protect Jewish students and staff", adding that the findings were a "serious concern".Lucy Powell, education secretary in England, said the findings in the CST report were "deeply troubling". "We expect universities to take a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism, and are providing training to help university staff identify and respond to incidents swiftly," she said.The CST defines an antisemitic incident as "university-related" if it concerns a student, member of staff or academic at a UK university "in their academic or student capacity" - including on campus and online.In 2022-23, the last academic year before the 7 October attack, the CST recorded 53 incidents. That grew to 272 in 2023-24.A report from the charity examining the past two academic years says reported incidents fell in 2024-25 and but grew again in 2025-26.The most common type of incident recorded by CST over both years was abusive behaviour, including verbal abuse, comments made in person or online and antisemitic graffiti.Its report said that, for the first time, there were two occurrences of extreme violence in 2024-25.It said there were six reported assaults across both years, eight incidents of damage and desecration to Jewish property - five of which were in student accommodation - and ten threats.Around two-thirds of reported incidents involved antisemitic language or targeting alongside references to Israel, Gaza, Hamas, the 7 October attack, and the subsequent conflicts in the Middle East.The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.Israel launched a mass military offensive on Gaza in response which has killed around 74,000 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.The CST report said: "While criticism of Israel and Zionism is not inherently antisemitic, the data in this report continue to demonstrate that anti-Zionist language is frequently deployed in conjunction with hostility towards Jews and Jewish organisations."Mark Gardner, CST's chief executive, said "Jews are still facing a very serious campus antisemitism problem" and it was "particularly troubling that a growing proportion of the anti-Jewish actions involve university staff".He added that universities had "a duty to ensure that Jewish students and staff can study, work and participate on campus the same as anyone else".Raphi Leon, president of the Union of Jewish Students, said the report "must be a shot in the arm to boost action to support Jewish students and tackle antisemitism".Vivienne Stern, chief executive of UUK, said: "The rise in antisemitic incidents in the UK, including on university campuses, is a serious concern."Universities have a responsibility to protect Jewish students and staff from abuse, and to ensure that students and staff clearly understand where the expression of a strongly held view becomes antisemitism and harassment."She said UUK had worked with organisations including the CST on guidance for universities, but added there was "more to do, particularly in building confidence in the effectiveness of disciplinary processes".

schema.headline: Antisemitism on the rise at universities, charity warns

title: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed
description: In a bid to get her mum to open up, Helen decided "to try and be calm about this and open up the possibility she could trust me". Dale Richardson, a p
body: In a bid to get her mum to open up, Helen decided "to try and be calm about this and open up the possibility she could trust me". Dale Richardson, a police fraud protect officer, encourages families to be "curious but not confrontational". "I like to break it down... and listen to them and say, right, how did you meet? And what have they said?"Helen convinced her mum to allow her to speak to the scammer on a video call.She says she quickly spotted the deepfake as the image was "fuzzy" and his voice out of sync with his movements.Helen tried to convince her mum the man she was speaking to was not who he said he was but she did not believe her."She was saying I made her feel disgusted and ashamed," says Helen. "And that I should let her have her relationship and not intervene."Forensic linguist Dr Lis Carter, who is part of the Scam Secrets team, stresses the importance of being patient and careful with your words when trying to help loved ones who believe they are in a genuine relationship."Being a family member coming into that, you are 'destroying' that happiness." Unable to break her mum away from the scam, Helen turned to her bank. She had a lasting power of attorney, meaning she could act on behalf of her mum and set up safeguards for her accounts.Jim Winters, head of economic crime at Nationwide, says anyone who believes a family member is being scammed should contact their bank."They might be limited in what they can share with you for data privacy reasons, but they can take steps to safeguard that account," he says."Once we know that a customer is being defrauded we can spot the hallmarks very quickly and take steps to break that spell."To date, the bank that Helen's mum uses has returned £45,000 to her account.Though Helen changed her mum's phone number three times, she continued to give the new one to the scammers. Helen eventually replaced her mum's smartphone with one that could only do calls and texts. Winters also advises "completely resetting" a loved ones digital footprint by changing telephone numbers, email address and social media accounts."That's what makes you visible, that's what puts you out there. So taking steps to reset all of that is so important," he says.

schema.headline: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed

title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
description: Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it h
body: Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city."Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September."All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded."We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia. Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action."Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.The situation, he admitted, was very difficult."It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center."In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC."This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction. Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware."We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon. Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery."Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed."This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

schema.headline: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign

title: Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs
description: High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs.It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lake
body: High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs.It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lakes near Penrith, Cumbria, Pettigrews in Kelso, Scotland, Seaham in County Durham and Enfield, Greater London, though distribution operations would continue to run from the latter. The proposals will also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will also continue as a distribution centre for the business.The chain, which has headquarters in Newcastle, said its retail shops would not be affected by the proposed changes.The changes would take place over the next two-and-a-half years, with parts of Greggs' manufacturing processes relocating, the firm said.The range of products manufactured at its Clydesmill Glasgow and Manchester locations would be reduced and production of tinned bread at Gosforth would be stopped.Some products would also be sourced from specialist suppliers.Chief executive Roisin Currie said the company needed to "keep evolving alongside changing customer expectations".She said: "Greggs manufacturing and logistics network remains a key strength of the business, and these proposals are intended to strengthen our manufacturing network, improve efficiency and ensure we remain well placed for the future while continuing to deliver the quality, value and service our customers expect."The firm employs 33,000 people in the UK, the majority working in its stores.A consultation with staff is expected to start soon and the company said "no final decisions" had been made yet.The shake-up is expected to cost the firm about £60m, including disruption costs and redundancy payments.It said the plans would save it about £20m across the 2028 and 2029 financial years.The retail business said its sales grew by 7.7% in the three months to September 26, compared with the same period a year earlier.It said this represented progress in the face of "challenging market conditions", as consumer finances continued to come under pressure.The company said positive trading and continued cost control meant it expected a "modestly improved outcome" for 2026.Greggs opened 95 new shops and closed 38 in the year to date, taking its overall estate to 2,796 shops.Follow BBC North East on X, external and Facebook, external and BBC Cumbria on X, external and Facebook, external and both on Nextdoor and Instagram, external.

schema.headline: Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs

title: People troll my DIY but they just spur me on
description: DIY influencer Jasmine Gurney has documented an impressive and exhausting sounding list of tasks on Instagram. She has torn down partition walls, repl
body: DIY influencer Jasmine Gurney has documented an impressive and exhausting sounding list of tasks on Instagram. She has torn down partition walls, replaced flooring, erected a fence, insulated and boarded her loft, built an outdoor workshop, made custom cabinetry, moved plug sockets, made her son his first bed and has been building him a treehouse.Eight months pregnant, the former marketer is now racing to finish building a fitted wardrobe before the new baby arrives."I like proving people wrong," says Jasmine, 33, from Bedfordshire, who says she's been trolled by people questioning her techniques but they just "spur me on more"."I'm showing and empowering other women to do it," she says."I've shown me doing things whilst pregnant, I've had my firstborn strapped to me in a baby carrier while doing things. "I'm just showing that we are capable, we are interested in this sort of stuff and... we're sick of waiting around for six months for our husbands to pick up the tools and do it in most cases."

schema.headline: People troll my DIY but they just spur me on

title: Tribute to former Kirkcudbright schoolboy killed in Ukraine
description: 'He was deeply loved': Tribute to former UK school pupil killed in UkraineImage source, Petrov FamilyImage caption, Arkadii Petrov was a former pupil
body: 'He was deeply loved': Tribute to former UK school pupil killed in UkraineImage source, Petrov FamilyImage caption, Arkadii Petrov was a former pupil of Kirkcudbright Academy ByGiancarlo RinaldiSouth Scotland reporterUpdated 4 hours agoA former pupil at a Scottish high school has been killed in action on the frontline in Ukraine. Arkadii Petrov and his family moved to Dumfries and Galloway when he was a teenager, following Russia's invasion in 2022. He attended Kirkcudbright Academy before returning to Ukraine to fight and was killed in action in the east of the country. His mother, Liudmyla, said he was "funny, bright, very charismatic and full of life" and had been an "incredibly loving brother" to his younger sisters and brother.Image source, Petrov FamilyImage caption, Arkadii studied for a year in Edinburgh before heading back to UkraineShe said the family had been told on 22 September that her eldest son had been killed in a combat mission on 18 September - just two days before he would have turned 21.As well as attending Kirkcudbright Academy, he also went to the University of Edinburgh for a year before interrupting his studies to return to Ukraine."Ukraine was the country he loved more than anything," said his mother."As the war continued, I could see him becoming more serious."He followed everything that was happening in Ukraine very closely and felt that he could not simply continue his normal life while other Ukrainians were defending the country where he was born."Image source, Petrov FamilyImage caption, The young soldier was killed two days before his 21st birthdayHe worked as a combat medic and drone operator and was wounded on a number of occasions in battle."Arkadii was sincere, brave and very honest - he had no falseness in him," said Liudmyla."But to us he was never only a soldier or his call sign, Arka."He was our Arkadii - my son, a brother, a grandson, a young man with books, music, jokes, dreams and an entire life that should have been ahead of him."She said he adored his sisters, Avrora and Kapitolina, and his younger brother Aaron."Wherever he was, he carried his family with him," added his mother.After his death, the family travelled from Scotland to Ukraine to arrange his funeral."The hardest thing for me is knowing that I will never again see his living face, hear his voice or hold him," said Liudmyla."I also grieve for the future he was meant to have - his dreams, his family one day, the children he might have had."However, she said she was also "enormously proud" of her son."He loved Ukraine more than anything, and he gave his life defending its freedom," she said."I want people to remember not simply that another young soldier died in Ukraine, but that Arkadii was a whole person, deeply loved, with a family, a childhood, a future and dreams."He was our son, our pride, and I want his name and his life to be remembered."Image source, Petrov FamilyImage caption, Arkadii's mother said she wanted his name to be rememberedPeter Kormylo, archivist at the Ukrainian Prisoner of War chapel in Lockerbie where Petrov attended services, said the whole community was upset by the death of a young man. He described Arkadii as a "very pleasant young man" who had arrived in Scotland with his mother and three younger siblings - one brother and two sisters.However, he said he had always been keen to go back to Ukraine and fight."All I can say about the boy is, having met him on a few occasions, he was a very courteous young man and quite a serious young man," he said."The last time I remember him being at the chapel I found him, when everyone had gone, sitting in the chapel writing a couple of what looked like letters - but in actual fact were prayers."He was a deep thinker and obviously felt the need to do what many Ukrainians are doing and that's fulfill their patriotic duty."Image source, James TowillImage caption, Petrov regularly attended services at the Ukrainian chapel near LockerbieKormylo said Arkadii's death was sad news for the wider Ukrainian community in the south of Scotland."He came here, at 16 or 17 years old with his mother, they were refugees," he said."They didn't know what the future would bring, but he did believe in Ukraine's eventual victory."He was a teenager maturing here and obviously gathered his own thoughts and decided to make a very adult decision."So the community is quite upset, as you would guess, everyone feels this pain."Anthony Tuffery, rector at Arkadii's old school, said everyone at Kirkcudbright Academy was saddened to hear of his death."Although he was only at the school for one year to complete his S6 studies, he was a polite, respectful and hardworking young man," he said."We would like to pass on our deepest sympathies to his family and friends and our thoughts are with them at this incredibly difficult time."

schema.headline: Tribute to former Kirkcudbright schoolboy killed in Ukraine

title: Gold beetles to Darwin's finds - the 70 million museum artefacts going online
description: Researchers are using AI to create a vast digital museum of millions of specimens from collections across the UK that they say could "supercharge" our
body: Researchers are using AI to create a vast digital museum of millions of specimens from collections across the UK that they say could "supercharge" our understanding of the natural world.People will eventually be able to see around 70 million animals, plants, fossils and rocks from their phones and computers.Robots and AI are being used to scan and analyse the specimens - some collected centuries ago - speeding up the digitisation process from hundreds of years to a decade. The new digital museum will enable researchers to understand how the UK has changed over the entire history of our planet and predict future changes to the climate, food supplies and species loss.The resource will be something that the public can access and enjoy too, says Dr Joanna Dunster, who is an associate director of the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) - part of the UK Research and Innovation Agency which is funding the project."I'm looking forward to exploring the resource with my four-year-old son, whose knowledge of science is little, but enthusiasm is great," she told BBC News.Some specimens are already searchable on the database, but they represent only a fraction of the country's collections, mostly from a handful of large institutions such as the Natural History Museum and the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. New funding will open drawers and cupboards in institutions across the UK to include millions more plants, animals and fossils."We need to make these collections openly accessible instead of sitting where they can rarely be reached," Dunster said.The public and researchers will be able to see the full diversity of the natural world, from the unusual - like the blind tripod fish that props itself on the seafloor, to the historical - a horse tooth recovered by Charles Darwin around 1833 from northeast Argentina. The resource is called the Distributed System of Scientific Collections, external (DiSSCo UK) and is led by the Natural History Museum. Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Kevin Church/BBCImage caption, Many specimens have scientific labels handwritten decades ago which can now be read more easily and digitally capturedSlide 1 of 5, A single preserved beetle is mounted on a long pin against a soft, pale purple background. The insect is shown side-on, facing left. Its body is dark brown to black, long and slightly flattened, with several irregular cream-coloured markings along its wing cases. Fine antennae project from its head, while six slender legs curl beneath its body. Several small paper labels hang below the beetle on the pin. One handwritten label appears to include the species name Cicindela, while printed labels record collection details and a museum reference number. A second pin with a rounded silver head stands just behind the specimen., Many specimens have scientific labels handwritten decades ago which can now be read more easily and digitally capturedScanning the specimens is not a trivial process. Not only does each one need to be photographed, but the tiny labels containing important scientific information, often handwritten, sometimes centuries ago, also have to be recorded. The team involved calculated that it would have taken hundreds of years to do this manually, but using robots and AI this process can now be done in a decade, according to Sarah Addezio, the DiSSCo UK's programme delivery director."What we're able to do now is connect and analyse that information at a scale that's unprecedented and has not been possible before."One hundred museums, botanic gardens, universities and other organisations are involved in the project. The specimens to go under the cameras will not be the big beasties: there are no whales or dinosaurs in the opening phase, which begins in Wales and Scotland. Beetles, butterflies, moths, flies, pressed flowers and ferns will go first - the small, less glamorous material that actually hold the best record of how the country around them has changed.In Cardiff, the team will scan around half a million insect and plant specimens, from large, showy butterflies down to flies you could lose on a fingertip, which turn out to be among the most sensitive indicators of a healthy landscape.In Scotland, the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh and National Museums Scotland hold 13 million specimens between them, the UK's second-largest natural science collection. Together with 50 smaller Scottish collections, the collections span from sea level to the tops of mountains - two centuries of change in the plants and insects of every kind of Scottish landscape.Jenny Geroni, who is the head of Natural Sciences and Research at the Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales, said it will be a chance to showcase material from across the country. "Each collection is unique. We have a lot of Welsh material that is not held anywhere else."By taking material from across the UK, it also allows us to build a good picture of what is going on across the whole country. And everyone adding their world collections will build a much stronger picture of what is going on elsewhere," Geroni told BBC News.Dr Vincent Smith, a research leader at the Natural History Museum in London, says it will "supercharge" research into the natural world."Natural history collections record long periods of change, often through really fundamental periods, such as the Industrial Revolution. Our collections chart those changes and so you can see what's happened before," he said.And, crucially, he added "start to predict what's going to happen next".By bringing together this large collection of specimens, researchers can refine their computer models of how the natural world will change in the future - studying how  climate change and other development choices will impact species loss. DiSSCo UK will also help scientists prepare for future challenges - by uploading more fossils and rock material it will aid research into minerals needed for green technology.

schema.headline: Gold beetles to Darwin's finds - the 70 million museum artefacts going online

title: Endometriosis trial gives hope to millions of women in pain like me
description: Image source, Charlotte McCannImage caption, Charlotte McCann said the trial gave her hope for the futureByKen BanksNorth East Scotland reporterReport
body: Image source, Charlotte McCannImage caption, Charlotte McCann said the trial gave her hope for the futureByKen BanksNorth East Scotland reporterReporting fromAberdeenCharlotte McCann has been dealing with severe pain from endometriosis since she was 14. It became so intolerable as an adult she had to leave her chosen career.She would wake up in the night vomiting, and on some days Charlotte found she could not stand or get out of bed.It is a myth that endometriosis is a painful period condition - rather, it is a system-wide inflammatory disease where cells, similar to those which line the womb, start to grow in other parts of the body. This can be on the bowel or in the lungs - and the cells multiply, creating raw and angry sores.Those affected can wait years for diagnosis, and there is no cure - meaning women are left grappling with debilitating pain that can affect their relationships, work, education and mental health.Now age 27, Charlotte hopes a new pain management programme for the condition, which is being trialled as part of a £2.3m study, might help others in her position.The UK-wide study, led by the University of Aberdeen and NHS Grampian, will include pain medication alongside other treatments such as physiotherapy, and will investigate whether a personalised plan can improve quality of life.Charlotte, from Huntly in Aberdeenshire, is currently living with stage 4 endometriosis, external.She had to abandon her career in corporate finance due to the pain, and now works as a freelance pet-sitter when she can."I would wake up in the night vomiting and I was always worried that maybe my appendix had burst or I had a kidney infection or something like that," she recalled."The pain would come on so strong, I wouldn't be able to even sit up straight, I wouldn't be able to stand up."It was heavily disrupting my life. I couldn't focus on anything, and I couldn't sleep or eat because of the pain. "There's no way I could continue my nine-to-five job when I could barely sit up."Charlotte said she had years of not knowing what was wrong, until an MRI scan confirmed endometriosis.It affected her bladder, and has spread to other parts of her body."I am now on very strong opioid painkillers to try to get on top of the pain, but they make me feel very sick, to the point I can't eat, so I have lost a lot of weight now as well," she said.Charlotte described being in so much pain that there are days when she cannot get out of bed.She also has to use walking aids to get around due to the pain in her back brought on by her endometriosis symptoms.She tried surgery to remove the tissue in question, but the symptoms returned.Asked about the new trial, Charlotte said she was optimistic."Endometriosis has had a huge impact on my life, and I am delighted to hear that they are looking at new ways to help the millions of women who are suffering with this every single day."What does the trial involve?Preparatory work has now begun for the five-year study, which is being funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).Once participants are recruited, they will take part in a 12-week personalised programme - called an endometriosis-specific pain management programme (e-PMP).The project will evaluate whether this strategy can offer more effective treatment for women who find their pain is not adequately controlled by surgery or medication.It includes cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)-informed psychotherapy, specialist physiotherapy, guidance on relationships, intimacy and communication, and medication to reduce side effects.Pre-menopausal women will either receive the new programme alongside existing standard care, or existing standard care alone, with the results of each approach then compared.Eligible participants will be recruited to the study by their specialist.Consultant gynaecologist Dr Lucky Saraswat, an honorary senior lecturer at the university, and lead for Aberdeen Endometriosis Centre at NHS Grampian, is heading the study.Image caption, Dr Lucky Saraswat is leading the new study"Endometriosis is one of the most common yet under researched causes of chronic pain," she said. "Many women continue to suffer even after surgery or medication."This study will help us understand whether a tailored, interdisciplinary pain management programme can offer meaningful, long term improvements in quality of life."If effective, e-PMP could become a vital new treatment option, particularly for women who wish to avoid repeated surgery or hormonal therapies, or who are planning a pregnancy."'Revolutionise care'Alongside the clinical results, the study will also aim to assess cost effectiveness.Prof Anthony Gordon, director of NIHR's health technology assessment programme, said many women could face years of "agonising" symptoms with few long-term options."High-quality research is essential to break this cycle and deliver treatment that addresses the full, complex impact of endometriosis," he said."By evaluating tailored, non-surgical pain management, this trial could revolutionise care - providing desperately needed support, improving daily lives, and offering long-term relief when standard treatments haven't worked."Emma Cox, chief executive of Endometriosis UK, added: "Symptoms of endometriosis including chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on someone's physical and mental health, and research is vital to helping improve management and treatment options."We welcome this much-needed research and look forward to working with the team to see how an endometriosis specific pain management programme could support those with the disease in the future."

schema.headline: Endometriosis trial gives hope to millions of women in pain like me

title: Drumcree dispute: More talks due to take place at Hillsborough
description: More talks over Drumcree dispute as stalemate continuesImage caption, Portadown District Lodge made their way from Drumcree Church and were stopped by
body: More talks over Drumcree dispute as stalemate continuesImage caption, Portadown District Lodge made their way from Drumcree Church and were stopped by police officers on Tuesday nightByLuke SprouleLyndsey TelfordBBC News NIMark SimpsonCommunity correspondent and Jayne McCormackPolitical correspondentUpdated 19 minutes agoThe Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, is holding further talks with community leaders on Wednesday over the controversial Drumcree march.It comes after lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition issued a fresh legal bid to try to prevent the march from going ahead.Members of the Orange Order are still waiting to begin their permitted parade, which was due to take place on Sunday, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.The residents' appeal will be the latest challenge to the march, which was given the go ahead after three separate legal hearings over the course of 13 hours late on Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday morning.Wednesday's talks at Hillsborough Castle are taking place in an upstairs room which, under normal circumstances, is used as a sitting room.The Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition and the Portadown Orange Order will wait in separate rooms before going upstairs for talks with the secretary of state.Senior members from the Orange Order have arrived, with Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson and Deputy District Master Alastair Power accompanied by loyalist activist Jamie Bryson, who has acted as a legal adviser for the lodge.All three made no comment on arrival.It is understood Bryson has not been part of the discussions with Sir Chris and has been waiting in a separate room.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Senior members from the Orange Order arrived at Hillsborough Castle on WednesdayThe discussions are a form of proximity talks, with the two sides not meeting face-to-face but both being under the same roof.Wednesday's discussions are the third day in a row that Hillsborough talks have taken place.At this stage there is no sign of progress but the fact that both sides are still engaged in discussions is being seen by government officials as a positive.Keeping the talks going, however, remains a challenge with neither side showing a willingness to compromise.Image caption, A police Land Rover remained near Drumcree church on Wednesday morningA group of protesters remain at the Garvaghy Road on Wednesday.Members of the Orange Order left Drumcree Church overnight - for the first time since the stand off began - but Deputy District Master Alastair Power returned on Wednesday morning.He said other members would also be there throughout the day.There was another attempt by Portadown District Lodge to walk the route at 22:10 BST on Tuesday.Accompanied by DUP MP Carla Lockhart, Power asked the police if they could facilitate their parade. The answer was no.The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in almost 30 years after a series of legal challenges.Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.What happened on Tuesday?Both the Orange Order and members of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition also met Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle on Tuesday.Speaking on his way into the talks, Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, said "reroute the sectarian parade, that's it".Speaking after a separate meeting with the secretary of state, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said the talks had been "positive and constructive".Image caption, A crowd gathered outside St John the Baptist church hall on the Garvaghy Road on Tuesday nightLater, hundreds of people attended a meeting beside St John the Baptist Church on the Garvaghy Road for an update on the talks process. Speaking to the media outside the hall, Mac Cionnaith said the only person the residents had left to meet was PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher. He said he will be waiting for Boutcher to let him know when the meeting would happen, adding: "Or is he going to hide behind a wall of uniforms of police in riot gear?"Image caption, Supporters of the Orange Order gathered for a rally at Portadown on Tuesday Meanwhile, the Portadown district master told hundreds of supporters at an outdoor rally in the town that unionist leaders needed to keep pressure on the secretary of state and chief constable and that the law must be "respected and applied".Nigel Dawson said: "Tonight, my position, our position, is very, very clear. The chief constable, who is responsible for ensuring the law is complied in this country, must apply the law. "He must respect the High Court judgement and he must deliver us safely and securely back to Carleton Street Orange Hall via the Garvaghy Road because that's what the Parade's Commission said and that is what a High Court has said. "He needs to deliver that now."Sinn Féin have called on the Irish government to intervene in the dispute.How did we get here?The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident.However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas.The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders.The row reemerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission - the organisation formed during the Drumcree dispute to decide on contentious marches during Northern Ireland's parading season - was overturned.On Friday, following 28 years of unsuccessful applications, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested.However that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go ahead just hours before it was due to take place.What is the Drumcree parade? Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Protesters spent more than a day along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of pointsThe Drumcree dispute was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes during the 1990s, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland.In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision upheld until Friday.

schema.headline: Drumcree dispute: More talks due to take place at Hillsborough
